# Opening: the child had no biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary's womb by the Holy Ghost, with no human male contributing. Joseph was his legal and supposed father, not his begetter. The case is built from the KJV text, link by link.

---

## 1. Mary was a virgin when she conceived

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."
**[L2]** The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin, a maiden who has not known a man." Luke uses it twice in this one verse.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097) means "to know." Here it is the idiom for sexual knowledge, as in Matthew 1:25, "knew her not."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." This quotes **[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
**[L2]** The Hebrew in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959), "a young woman of marriageable age." Matthew's Greek, *parthenos*, fixes the sense as "virgin" in the quotation. Mary's own words in Luke 1:34 confirm it.

**[L4]** Mary is called *parthenos* by Luke, says "I know not a man," and is the fulfilment of the sign Matthew quotes. She had had no sexual relations when the angel announced the conception. A conception with a human father would need that union, so the announcement itself excludes it.

## 2. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost," not of a man

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** The preposition is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from the source of." The Spirit is named as the source, and the time is "before they came together."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** "Conceived" is *gennaō* (G1080), "to beget, to bring forth." The Greek reads *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*, "that which is begotten in her is out of the Holy Spirit." *Gennaō* is the verb of fathering, and here it is attributed to the Spirit.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L2]** *episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." The "therefore" (*dio*) makes the divine agency the reason for the title "Son of God."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 both name the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception. Luke 1:35 gives the agent and the result with "therefore." Where Scripture names one source of the begetting, no second begetter is assigned.

## 3. Joseph's fatherhood is legal and supposed

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
**[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543, from *nomizō*) means "was deemed, was reckoned by custom or law." It marks a view held by others, not a fact.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
**[L2]** The relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular, so the one born is from Mary alone. The verb also changes. Each earlier line in the genealogy uses active "begat" (*egennēsen*), as in **[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac." The line ends with the passive *egennēthē*, "was born," attached to Mary and not to Joseph.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man... was minded to put her away privily." He did not claim paternity, and the angel had to overturn his suspicion.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern with a feminine "of whom," and Luke 3:23 adds "as was supposed." Together they show Joseph was father by legal reckoning and marriage, and not the begetter.

## 4. Pressed texts that call Joseph "father" or Jesus "seed of David"

**[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"
**[L3]** Luke 3:23 supplies the corrective, "as was supposed." John 6:42 records what the speakers said, not what the narrator affirms.

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Mary says this in the household's ordinary usage. The next verse answers it.
**[L3]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?"
**[L4]** Jesus answers Mary's "thy father" with "my father's business," the temple. He redirects the title to God.

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
**[L2]** *sperma* (G4690) means "seed, offspring, descendant." In Scripture it covers descent through a woman.
**[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The Greek *genomenon ek gynaikos* names the woman as the human source.
**[L3]** Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." David, a thousand years earlier, is called "father," so the word can mean forefather and does not require an immediate begetter.
**[L4]** Paul's "according to the flesh" in Romans 1:3 is joined by Galatians 4:4 to "of a woman." The Davidic descent is therefore through the mother. Joseph's Davidic line (Matthew 1:20, "son of David") supplies the legal right of inheritance.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Mary was a virgin at the conception. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:27 and Luke 1:34 ("I know not a man"), with [L2] *parthenos* (virgin) and *ginōskō* (to know sexually), and [L3] Matthew 1:23 quoting Isaiah 7:14.
2. The conception was from the Holy Ghost as its source. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 ("of the Holy Ghost"), with [L2] *ek* (out of) and *gennaō* (to beget), and [L3] Luke 1:35 ("overshadow thee... therefore").
3. Joseph was the supposed and legal father only. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 ("as was supposed"), with [L2] *enomizeto* (was deemed), and [L3] Matthew 1:16 ("of whom was born Jesus").
4. "Father" and "seed of David" texts do not make Joseph the begetter. Footing: [L1] Romans 1:3 and John 6:42, with [L2] *sperma* (seed, descendant), and [L3] Luke 1:32, Luke 2:49 and Galatians 4:4.
5. Christ had no biological human father. Footing: links 1 to 4, with [L1] Luke 1:35, [L2] *episkiazō* (to overshadow), and [L3] Matthew 1:20.

# Challenger: the seed is David's by the flesh, and the father the text names is Joseph

**Position.** [L4] Jesus Christ had a biological father, Joseph, the man the text names as his father, of the house and lineage of David. The promised seed comes out of a man's loins. The angel's words in Luke 1:35 and Matthew 1:20 are words of empowerment, presence and covenant origin. None of the defender's five links agrees with the meaning of the verses below.

---

## MY CHAIN: C1 to C5

**C1. The promised seed comes out of a man's body.**
- **[L1]** 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom."
- **[L2]** The Hebrew *me'eh* (H4578) means "inward parts, bowels." The seed comes out of David's own body.
- **[L3]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- **[L2]** The Greek *osphys* (G3751) means "loins." It is the same word as Hebrews 7:10, "he was yet in the loins of his father."
- **[L3]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- **[L2]** The Greek *sperma* (G4690) means "seed." The Greek *kata sarka* means "according to the flesh."
- **[L4]** Peter applies the loins oath to Christ. Hebrews uses the same loins word of a father. So the seed promised to David, and fulfilled in Christ, comes out of a father's loins.

**C2. The text names one man as the child's father.**
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- **[L2]** The Greek is *ho patēr sou*, "thy father." Mary says it of Joseph.
- **[L3]** Luke 2:41: "Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover." Here the narrator speaks, not the crowd.
- **[L2]** The Greek *goneis* (G1118) means "parents, those who begat."
- **[L3]** Luke 2:4: Joseph "was of the house and lineage of David."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David."
- **[L4]** The narrator says "his parents." Mary says "thy father." Each of these voices names Joseph. Joseph is also the Davidic man in the house.

**C3. Israel reckons a man by his father's house.**
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
- **[L2]** The Greek *prodēlos* (G4271) means "plainly evident." The Greek *anatellō* (G393) means "to spring up, arise."
- **[L3]** Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."
- **[L3]** Ezra 2:62 shows what happens otherwise. The children of Barzillai's son-in-law were "called after their name" through the wife's house (Ezra 2:61). They "sought their register ... but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."
- **[L4]** A tribe is evident by the father's house. The register refused descent reckoned through a wife's house. So Judah's descent is evident through the father.

**C4. The union happened within the espousal.**
- **[L1]** Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband." Matthew 1:20: "Mary thy wife."
- **[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:24-25: Joseph "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- **[L2]** The Greek *heōs hou* means "until."
- **[L4]** The text's stated means of conceiving is a husband knowing his wife (Genesis 4:1). Joseph and Mary were husband and wife from the espousal (Matthew 1:19-20; Deuteronomy 22:24). The "till" of Matthew 1:25 sets the abstinence after the taking and during the pregnancy. So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins.

**C5. Keystone.**
- **[L4]** Footed on C1 to C4: Christ had a biological father, Joseph, the named Davidic father.

---

## PRESSES AGAINST THE DEFENDER'S CHAIN

### Against D1 (virgin at the conception)

**First press: Luke 1:31 and 1:34.**
- **[L1]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb." The verb is future.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:34: "seeing I know not a man."
- **[L2]** The Greek *ou ginōskō* means "I know not." It is present active indicative, so it gives her state as she spoke.
- **[L4]** A present state at the announcement does not describe the conception that verse 31 puts in the future.

**Second press: Isaiah 7:14 in its own setting.**
- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14 uses *ha-almah* (H5959), "the young woman." This word stands in 7 verses.
- **[L3]** The Hebrew has a virgin-word, *bethulah* (H1330), "virgin." It is used in Genesis 24:16: "a virgin, neither had any man known her." Isaiah 7:14 does not use it.
- **[L3]** Isaiah 7:16 bounds the sign: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings."
- **[L3]** Isaiah 8:3-4 then follows: "she conceived, and bare a son ... For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father."
- **[L4]** Isaiah's own sign has a child who cries "My father." It does not carry "no man" into Matthew 1:23.

### Against D2 ("of the Holy Ghost")

**Press: the pattern of *ek* with God or the Spirit.**
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived [Gr. begotten] in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** The Greek *ek* means "out of, from." Here it stands with *pneumatos hagiou*, "Holy Spirit."
- **[L3]** John 1:13: "born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **[L3]** 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God."
- **[L4]** In those rows, people with natural fathers are "born of God." That is an origin in God that stands beside a natural father. Romans 1:3 adds "according to the flesh" when flesh is meant, and Matthew 1:20 does not add it.

**Press: the verbs of Luke 1:35.**
- **[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
- **[L2]** The Greek *eperchomai* (G1904) means "to come upon." It stands in 10 verses.
- **[L3]** Acts 1:8 uses the same verb: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you." This is said of the apostles.
- **[L2]** The Greek *episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." It stands in 5 verses.
- **[L3]** Luke 9:34 uses the same verb of the transfiguration cloud. Acts 5:15 uses it of Peter's shadow.
- **[L4]** These verbs speak of empowerment and presence at their other rows. They do not name a begetter.

**Press: the title "Son of God."**
- **[L1]** Luke 1:32 gives the title and the throne first: "the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." This comes before Mary's question in verse 34.
- **[L3]** 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son ... I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father." In one verse, Solomon is David's son and God's son.
- **[L3]** Acts 13:33 sets "this day have I begotten thee" at the resurrection: "he hath raised up Jesus again."
- **[L4]** The title is the Davidic covenant title. It stands beside a natural father, as it did for Solomon.

### Against D3 (Joseph the supposed and legal father only)

**Press: the genealogy's own "of" with women.**
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:5: "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth."
- **[L2]** The Greek is *ek tēs*, "of her." In these lines a named father begets, and the mother is named with *ek*.
- **[L4]** The "of whom" of Matthew 1:16 is feminine because Mary is the mother named. The genealogy uses the same construction where a father begets.

**Press: what "as was supposed" means.**
- **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- **[L2]** The Greek *enomizeto* (G3543) means "was reckoned by custom or law." This is the defender's own gloss.
- **[L3]** Acts 16:13 uses the same verb form: "where prayer was wont to be made." Nothing false is reckoned there.
- **[L4]** The verb gives no verdict of its own. The reckoning the law knows is "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2).

**Press: Matthew 1:19.**
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L2]** The Greek *eboulēthē* means "was minded, intended."
- **[L4]** The verse states an intent and two grounds for it. It has no verb of knowing, so the defender's "suspicion" is not in the verse.

### Against D4 ("father" and "seed of David")

**Press: "my Father's business."**
- **[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
- **[L3]** Luke 2:51: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them."
- **[L3]** 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son." God says this of David's own son.
- **[L4]** God's fatherhood stands beside David's in 2 Samuel 7:14. "My Father's business" stands beside "thy father" in the same way, and Luke does not withdraw "his parents."

**Press: "seed" said of a woman.**
- **[L1]** The rows where "seed" is said of a woman in the offspring sense are Genesis 3:15, Genesis 16:10 (Hagar), Genesis 24:60 (Rebekah) and Isaiah 54:3 (Zion).
- **[L4]** None of these four is Davidic.

**Press: who is "of the house of David."**
- **[L1]** Luke 1:27: "espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."
- **[L2]** The Greek *ex oikou David* means "of the house of David." It follows *andri*, "a man."
- **[L3]** Luke 1:36 calls Elisabeth Mary's "cousin," and Luke 1:5 places Elisabeth "of the daughters of Aaron."
- **[L4]** The house of David is said of Joseph. Mary's kin named in Luke is of Aaron.

**Press: "made of a woman."**
- **[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman."
- **[L3]** Job 14:1: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days."
- **[L3]** Matthew 11:11 says the same of John: "born of women." Luke 1:13 names John's father.
- **[L4]** "Of a woman" is the mortality idiom. It is said of men whose fathers are named.

**My question to the defender:** According to Hebrews 7:14, how is it evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda? Given the law, Numbers 1:2 and 1:18.

---

# Round 2: link round, with the answer to the challenger's question

## The challenger's question: how is it evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda?

**[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
**[L2]** *prodēlos* (G4271) means "plainly evident." *anatellō* (G393) means "to spring up."
**[L3]** Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."
**[L3]** Luke 2:4-5: Joseph went up "because he was of the house and lineage of David: To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife."

**[L4]** I never denied that Joseph's house is the legal register. Link 3 says Joseph was father "by legal reckoning." Numbers 1:18 reckons by the father's house, and Luke 2:4 puts Joseph and Mary in that house at the enrolment. So Judah is evident in the public register. That is a statement about reckoning, and it does not say who begat. The fleshly descent from David is a further matter, answered in LINK 5.

---

## LINK ROUND

### LINK 1: SUPPORTED

The premise: "Matthew's Greek, *parthenos*, fixes the sense as 'virgin' in the quotation."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
**[L2]** *parthenos* (G3933) is the word Matthew's Greek uses for the Isaiah quotation. Luke uses the same word of Mary in Luke 1:27.
**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
**[L2]** *ʿalmāh* (H5959) is glossed in the lexicon sheet "a lass (as veiled or private); damsel, maid, virgin." The KJV renders it "virgin" in this very verse. The same verse says *ʾôwth* (H226), "sign, miracle, prodigy."

**Pressed: Genesis 24:16** ("a virgin, neither had any man known her").
**[L2]** The word there is *bᵉthûwlâh* (H1330). The text still adds "neither had any man known her," so the clause, not the noun alone, carries the exclusion.
**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." This is the same Rebekah, called by *ʿalmāh* (H5959) in that verse, though verse 16 had called her *bᵉthûwlâh*. So the two Hebrew words are used of the same woman, a virgin.

**Pressed: Isaiah 7:16** ("before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings"), **Isaiah 8:3** ("I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son") and **Isaiah 8:4** ("before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother").
**[L2]** Isaiah 8:3 names her *nᵉbîyʾâh* (H5031), "prophetess," and not *ʿalmāh*. The two verses are therefore not shown to be one woman.
**[L3]** Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet." Matthew applies the word as fulfilled in Mary, whatever nearer sign Isaiah's day had.
**[L4]** Matthew gives *parthenos* (virgin) for *ʿalmāh*. Isaiah 7:14 calls the event a *sign* (*ʾôwth*), and Genesis 24:16 and 24:43 show *ʿalmāh* applied to a virgin. That is the footing for "virgin" in the quotation. The sign's near-term setting in Isaiah 7:16 does not erase the word's sense.

### LINK 2: SUPPORTED

The premise: "A conception with a human father would need that union, so the announcement itself excludes it."

**[L1]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb." **[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097) is present active, "I know." *Ou ginōskō* gives her state, and verse 34 asks how the future event of verse 31 will come to be, given that state.
**[L1]** Luke 1:27 says she is "espoused," so marriage with Joseph was already expected. If a natural conception in due course were meant, there would be no question to ask.
**[L1]** Luke 1:35 answers with no mention of a husband: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** *synerchomai* (G4905) means "to come together."
**[L4]** The question in Luke 1:34 only has force if the conception is to take place without her knowing a man. The answer in Luke 1:35 gives only the Holy Ghost's action. Matthew 1:18 then fixes the pregnancy before the coming together. The future tense of 1:31 and the present tense of 1:34 therefore meet in 1:35 and 1:18.

**On C4, which presses the same point:**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
**[L4]** Genesis 4:1 gives the ordinary means ("Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived"). Matthew 1:18 places the pregnancy "before they came together," and 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" until the birth. The text itself denies the husband's knowing at the only time the child could have been conceived. "Wife" in Matthew 1:20 and Deuteronomy 22:24 is the espousal's legal status and says nothing about knowing.

### LINK 3: SUPPORTED

The premise: "*Gennaō* is the verb of fathering, and here it is attributed to the Spirit."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The KJV margin reads "Gr. begotten."
**[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080) is the verb the KJV's own margin glosses as "begotten."

**Pressed: John 1:13** ("born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God") **and 1 John 5:1** ("Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God").
**[L2]** In both verses the word is *gennaō* (G1080). In 1 John 5:1 it is used for "him that begat" and "begotten of him," so the verb is the begetting verb.
**[L4]** John 1:13 sets "of God" against "the will of man," and the contrast runs both ways. The birth "of God" there is a new birth and is not a first conception. Matthew 1:20 speaks of the one begotten "in her," and Matthew 1:18 gives the time as "before they came together." So *ek* with God excludes the man in John 1:13, and the same excludes him in Matthew 1:20. 1 John 5:1 describes believers' second birth, which stands beside a natural first birth, and nothing in Matthew 1:18 or 1:20 describes a second one.

**Pressed: Acts 1:8** ("the Holy Ghost is come upon you") **and Luke 9:34** ("there came a cloud, and overshadowed them").
**[L4]** The begetting claim rests on Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35's "that holy thing which shall be born of thee," not on the verbs *eperchomai* (G1904, "to come upon") or *episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") alone. Luke 1:35 says the one born is "of thee" and gives "therefore" as the reason for "Son of God." No man appears in the verse.

**Pressed: 1 Chronicles 28:6 and Acts 13:33.**
**[L3]** Hebrews 1:5 quotes 2 Samuel 7:14 of Christ: "I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son." There, God is the Father by declaration. The question here is whether Luke 1:35's "therefore" gives a fleshly origin, and Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 answer it.

### LINK 4: SUPPORTED

The premise: "Together they show Joseph was father by legal reckoning and marriage, and not the begetter."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
**[L2]** The verb changes from *egennēsen*, "begat" (G1080, active), to *egennēthē*, "was born" (G1080, passive).

**Pressed: Matthew 1:3** ("Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar") **and Matthew 1:5** ("Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth").
